questions.answer: Sample B varies more: its MAD is 3.2, while Sample A's MAD is 0.8.
questions.solution: Distances from 50. Sample A: 2, 0, 2, 0, 0, which add to 4, so the MAD is 4 / 5 = 0.8. Sample B: 6, 6, 2, 2, 0, which add to 16, so the MAD is 16 / 5 = 3.2. Sample B varies more.

solve.answer: Sample B varies more: its MAD is 3.2, while Sample A's MAD is 0.8.
solve.work: A distances from 50: 2,0,2,0,0 sum 4, MAD 0.8. B: 6,6,2,2,0 sum 16, MAD 3.2. B varies more.

questions.skill: Compare the IQRs of two samples
questions.stem: Random samples of times: Group X has a median of 30 and an IQR of 6. Group Y has a median of 24 and an IQR of 14. Which statement is best supported?
choices: Group X's typical value is higher, and its middle half of values is more spread out.
Group X's typical value is higher, and its middle half of values is less spread out.
Group Y's typical value is higher, and its middle half of values is less spread out.
Group Y's typical value is higher, and its middle half of values is more spread out.
questions.answer: Group X's typical value is higher, and its middle half of values is less spread out.
questions.solution: The median of X (30) is greater than the median of Y (24), so X is typically higher. The IQR of X (6) is less than the IQR of Y (14), so X's middle half is less spread out.

solve.answer: Group X's typical value is higher, and its middle half of values is less spread out.
solve.work: X median 30 > 24; X IQR 6 < 14 so less spread.

questions.skill: Compare the IQRs of two samples
questions.stem: Random samples of the minutes students spent on a game one evening. Sample 1: 2, 6, 8, 10, 14, 18, 22, 30. Sample 2: 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 19. Find each quartile as the median of the lower half or the upper half of the 8 values. How much greater is the IQR of Sample 1 than the IQR of Sample 2?
questions.solution: Sample 1: the lower half is 2, 6, 8, 10 with median 7, and the upper half is 14, 18, 22, 30 with median 20, so the IQR is $20 - 7 = 13$. Sample 2: the lower half is 9, 10, 12, 13 with median 11, and the upper half is 15, 16, 18, 19 with median 17, so the IQR is $17 - 11 = 6$. The difference is $13 - 6 = 7$.

questions.skill: Compare the MADs of two samples
questions.stem: Two random samples of the number of points scored by two players each have a mean of 18. Player A: 10, 14, 20, 22, 24. Player B: 15, 16, 18, 20, 21. How many points greater is the MAD of Player A's sample than the MAD of Player B's sample?
questions.solution: Player A: distances from 18 are 8, 4, 2, 4, 6, which add to 24, so the MAD is 24 / 5 = 4.8. Player B: distances are 3, 2, 0, 2, 3, which add to 10, so the MAD is 10 / 5 = 2. The difference is 4.8 - 2 = 2.8.

solve.work: A sum 90 mean 18; distances 8,4,2,4,6 sum 24, MAD 4.8. B sum 90 mean 18; distances 3,2,0,2,3 sum 10, MAD 2. 4.8-2=2.8.

questions.skill: Compare the difference in means with the MAD
questions.stem: Sample A: 5, 7, 9, 11. Sample B: 13, 15, 17, 19. The two samples have the same MAD. The difference between the means is how many times that MAD?
questions.solution: Mean of A: 32 / 4 = 8. Mean of B: 64 / 4 = 16. Distances from the mean in A: 3, 1, 1, 3, so the MAD is 8 / 4 = 2. The difference in means is 16 - 8 = 8, and 8 / 2 = 4.

solve.work: A mean 8, distances 3,1,1,3, MAD 2. B mean 16, MAD 2. Difference 8; 8/2=4.

questions.skill: Compare the difference in means with the MAD
questions.stem: The means of two random samples of plant heights differ by 12 centimeters. The two samples have the same MAD, and the difference between the means is 3 times that MAD. What is the MAD, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The difference, 12, equals 3 times the MAD. So the MAD is 12 / 3 = 4 centimeters.

questions.skill: Draw an informal inference about two populations
questions.stem: Ben compares two random samples of quiz scores. The greatest score in Sample A is 98, and the greatest in Sample B is 91. He says, "So the students in population A did better than those in population B." What is the best response?
choices: He is right, because the greatest score shows which population did better.
He is wrong, because only the least score should be compared.
One greatest score does not show typical performance; he should compare centers and spreads.
He is right, because samples always describe the populations exactly.
questions.answer: One greatest score does not show typical performance; he should compare centers and spreads.
questions.solution: A single extreme value says little about the typical student. To compare populations, compare a measure of center (mean or median) and a measure of spread (MAD or IQR) of the samples.

solve.answer: One greatest score does not show typical performance; he should compare centers and spreads.
solve.work: A single maximum does not describe typical performance; compare centres and spreads.

questions.skill: Compare the means of two samples
questions.stem: Random samples of 5 daily step counts, in thousands, for two people. Person A: 20, 18, 22, 19, 21. Person B: 15, 17, 16, 18, 19. The value 32 is added to Person B's sample. How much greater is the mean of Person A's sample than the mean of Person B's new sample?
questions.solution: Person A: 100 / 5 = 20. Person B with 32 added: 85 + 32 = 117, and 117 / 6 = 19.5. The difference is 20 - 19.5 = 0.5.

questions.skill: Compare the difference in means with the MAD
questions.stem: Each pair of random samples has the means and MADs shown. Which pair gives the strongest evidence that the two populations have different means?
questions.solution: Compare the difference in means with the MAD. Means 50 and 62 with MAD 3: 12 is 4 times the MAD. With MAD 12 it is only 1 time the MAD, a difference of 2 with MAD 3 is under 1 time the MAD, and a difference of 6 with MAD 10 is under 1 time the MAD. The first pair is the strongest.

solve.work: Separation in MADs: 12/3=4; 12/12=1; 6/10=0.6; 2/3~0.67. Strongest: means 50 and 62, MADs 3.

questions.skill: Compare the IQRs of two samples
questions.stem: Random samples of the number of minutes students waited for lunch. Class A: 15, 7, 23, 12, 4, 19, 9, 14. Class B: 17, 11, 19, 14, 10, 18, 13, 15. How much greater is the IQR of Class A's sample than the IQR of Class B's sample?
questions.solution: In order, A: 4, 7, 9, 12, 14, 15, 19, 23. Lower half 4, 7, 9, 12 has median 8; upper half 14, 15, 19, 23 has median 17; IQR = 9. B: 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19. Lower half median 12, upper half median 17.5; IQR = 5.5. The difference is 9 - 5.5 = 3.5.

questions.skill: Compare the difference in means with the MAD
questions.stem: Dina compares two random samples. Sample 1 has a mean of 12.4 and a MAD of 4.1. Sample 2 has a mean of 11.9 and a MAD of 3.9. She says the populations are very different. What is the best response?
choices: The means differ by only 0.5, small compared with the MADs, so the evidence is weak.
The means differ by 0.5, which is large compared with the MADs, so she is right.
The means differ by 24.3, so she is right.
She is right, because Sample 1 has the larger mean and the larger MAD.
questions.answer: The means differ by only 0.5, small compared with the MADs, so the evidence is weak.
questions.solution: The means differ by 12.4 - 11.9 = 0.5. The MADs are about 4, so the difference is only about one eighth of a MAD. The samples overlap almost completely, so there is little evidence the populations differ.

solve.answer: The means differ by only 0.5, small compared with the MADs, so the evidence is weak.
solve.work: 12.4-11.9=0.5, about 0.12 of a MAD: weak evidence.

questions.skill: Compare the MADs of two samples
questions.stem: Random samples of the number of seconds it takes two machines to finish a job. Machine A: 12, 16, 20, 24. Machine B: 10, 12, 14, 16. How many times as great is the MAD of Machine A's sample as the MAD of Machine B's sample?
questions.solution: Machine A: mean 72 / 4 = 18; distances 6, 2, 2, 6; MAD = 16 / 4 = 4. Machine B: mean 52 / 4 = 13; distances 3, 1, 1, 3; MAD = 8 / 4 = 2. 4 / 2 = 2, so A's MAD is 2 times B's.

solve.work: A mean 18, distances 6,2,2,6, MAD 4. B mean 13, distances 3,1,1,3, MAD 2. 4/2=2.

questions.skill: Compare the medians of two samples
questions.stem: Random samples of the number of books read in a year. Group A: 31, 27, 35, 29, 38, 33. Group B: 24, 30, 26, 22, 28, 25. How many books greater is the median of Group A's sample than the median of Group B's sample?
questions.solution: With 6 values, the median is the mean of the middle two in order. A: 27, 29, 31, 33, 35, 38, so the median is (31 + 33) / 2 = 32. B: 22, 24, 25, 26, 28, 30, so the median is (25 + 26) / 2 = 25.5. The difference is 32 - 25.5 = 6.5.

questions.skill: Describe an event from its probability
questions.stem: Which word describes an event with a probability of 0?
questions.solution: A probability of 0 means the event can never happen. That is impossible.

questions.skill: Place an event on the 0 to 1 scale
questions.stem: What is the probability of an event that is certain to happen?
questions.solution: An event that is certain always happens, so its probability is 1, the top of the scale.

questions.skill: Choose a number that can be a probability
questions.stem: Which number could be the probability of an event?
questions.solution: A probability is a number from 0 to 1. 0.7 is in that range. 1.3 and $\frac{9}{8}$ are greater than 1, and -0.2 is less than 0.

questions.skill: Place an event on the 0 to 1 scale
questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed once. What is the probability that it lands on heads?
questions.solution: Heads and tails are equally likely, so heads is 1 out of 2 outcomes. The probability is $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.skill: Place an event on the 0 to 1 scale
questions.stem: A fair six-sided die has faces numbered 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 9?
questions.solution: There is no face with a 9, so rolling a 9 is impossible. Its probability is 0.

questions.skill: Describe an event from its probability
questions.stem: The probability of an event is 0.95. Which phrase best describes the event?
questions.solution: A probability near 1 means the event is very likely to happen. 0.95 is close to 1.

questions.skill: Describe an event from its probability
questions.stem: An event has a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$. Which phrase best describes it?
questions.solution: A probability of $\frac{1}{2}$ is halfway between 0 and 1. The event is just as likely to happen as not to happen.

questions.skill: Interpret a probability in a situation
questions.stem: The weather report says the probability of snow tomorrow is 0.1. What does this mean?
choices: Snow is certain to fall tomorrow.
Snow is just as likely as not tomorrow.
Snow is unlikely, but it could happen.
Snow cannot fall tomorrow at all.
questions.answer: Snow is unlikely, but it could happen.
questions.solution: 0.1 is close to 0, so snow is unlikely. It is not 0, so snow is still possible.

solve.answer: Snow is unlikely, but it could happen.
solve.work: 0.1 is near 0 but not 0: unlikely but possible.

questions.skill: Compare and order probabilities
questions.stem: Which probability belongs to the least likely event?
questions.solution: The smaller the probability, the less likely the event. The smallest of the four numbers is 0.2.

questions.skill: Find a probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.stem: A spinner has 5 equal sections. 2 of the sections are shaded. What is the probability that the spinner lands on a shaded section?
questions.solution: All 5 sections are equally likely and 2 are shaded, so the probability is $\frac{2}{5}$.

questions.skill: Choose a number that can be a probability
questions.stem: How many of these numbers could be the probability of an event? $0.4$, $1.2$, $-0.3$, $\frac{7}{5}$, $\frac{1}{8}$, $1$, $0$
questions.solution: A probability is from 0 to 1, including 0 and 1. These fit: 0.4, $\frac{1}{8}$, 1 and 0. The numbers 1.2 and $\frac{7}{5}$ are greater than 1, and -0.3 is less than 0. So 4 numbers could be probabilities.

questions.skill: Choose a number that can be a probability
questions.stem: Which statement about probabilities is true?
choices: It is a number between 0 and 1, but it can never equal 0 or 1.
It is a number between 0 and 1, and it can equal 0 or 1.
It is a number greater than 1 when the event is very likely.
It is any number, and a larger number means more likely.
questions.answer: It is a number between 0 and 1, and it can equal 0 or 1.
questions.solution: Probabilities are numbers from 0 to 1 and include both ends: 0 for an impossible event and 1 for a certain event.

solve.answer: It is a number between 0 and 1, and it can equal 0 or 1.

questions.skill: Place an event on the 0 to 1 scale
questions.stem: Which event has a probability closest to 0?
choices: You flip a fair coin and it lands on heads.
You roll a number less than 7 on a fair six-sided die.
You roll a 6 on a fair six-sided die.
You pick a blue marble from a bag of only red marbles.
questions.answer: You pick a blue marble from a bag of only red marbles.
questions.solution: Picking blue from a bag with only red marbles is impossible, so its probability is 0. The others are $\frac{1}{2}$, 1 and $\frac{1}{6}$.

solve.answer: You pick a blue marble from a bag of only red marbles.
solve.work: Blue from only red: probability 0 (closest to 0). Others 1/2, 1, 1/6.

questions.skill: Compare and order probabilities
questions.stem: Which list shows these probabilities in order from least likely to most likely: $\frac{3}{4}$, $0.2$, $\frac{1}{2}$, $0.05$?
questions.solution: Write each as a decimal: 0.75, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.05. From least to greatest: 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 0.75.

questions.skill: Interpret a probability in a situation
questions.stem: Dana is told that the probability her bus is late on a school day is 0.8. Which statement is the best interpretation?
choices: The bus is on time more often than it is late.
The bus is just as likely to be late as on time.
The bus will be late tomorrow for certain.
The bus is late more often than it is on time.
questions.answer: The bus is late more often than it is on time.
questions.solution: 0.8 is closer to 1 than to 0 and is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, so being late is likely. It is not 1, so it is not certain.

solve.answer: The bus is late more often than it is on time.
solve.work: 0.8 > 0.5: in the long run late more often than not.

questions.skill: Find a probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.stem: A bag holds 12 marbles: 9 red and 3 yellow. One marble is picked without looking. What is the probability that it is red?
questions.solution: There are 12 equally likely marbles and 9 are red. The probability is $\frac{9}{12}$ = $\frac{3}{4}$.

questions.skill: Find a probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sections. 7 of them are shaded. Which description of landing on a shaded section is correct?
choices: Neither likely nor unlikely, with probability $\frac{1}{2}$
questions.solution: The probability is $\frac{7}{8}$, which is close to 1. So landing on a shaded section is likely but not certain.

questions.skill: Place an event on the 0 to 1 scale
questions.stem: How many of these events have a probability of 1? (1) A fair coin lands on heads. (2) Two six-sided dice are rolled and their sum is at least 2. (3) A six-sided die is rolled and shows 0. (4) A six-sided die is rolled and shows a number less than 7.
questions.solution: Event (1) has probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and event (3) is impossible (probability 0). Two dice always add to at least 2, and a die always shows less than 7, so events (2) and (4) are certain. That is 2 events.

questions.skill: Compare and order probabilities
questions.stem: The probability that Team A wins a game is 0.35. The probability that Team B wins the same game is 0.65. There can be no tie. Which statement is true?
choices: Team A is more likely to win than Team B.
The two teams are equally likely to win.
Team B is more likely to win than Team A.
Team A is certain to win the game.
questions.answer: Team B is more likely to win than Team A.
questions.solution: A greater probability means a more likely event. 0.65 is greater than 0.35, so Team B is more likely to win. Neither probability is 1, so no team is certain to win.

solve.answer: Team B is more likely to win than Team A.

questions.skill: Choose a number that can be a probability
questions.stem: The number $\frac{n}{6}$ is the probability of an event, where n is a whole number. What is the greatest possible value of n?
questions.solution: A probability cannot be greater than 1. $\frac{n}{6}$ is at most 1 when n is at most 6. So the greatest n is 6.

questions.skill: Choose a number that can be a probability
questions.stem: The probability of event A is p. The probability of event B is twice as large, 2p. What is the greatest value that p could have?
questions.solution: Both p and 2p must be at most 1. The condition 2p is at most 1 means p is at most $\frac{1}{2}$. So the greatest value of p is $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.skill: Choose a number that can be a probability
questions.stem: Mia counted 12 outcomes that make an event happen out of 10 outcomes in all, and wrote the probability as $\frac{12}{10}$. What does this tell you?
choices: She made a counting mistake, because a probability cannot be greater than 1.
She is correct, because likely events have probabilities greater than 1.
She made a mistake, because a probability must be a whole number.
She is correct, because a probability can be any positive fraction.
questions.answer: She made a counting mistake, because a probability cannot be greater than 1.
questions.solution: The outcomes that make the event happen are part of all the outcomes, so there cannot be 12 of them out of 10. A probability is never greater than 1, and $\frac{12}{10}$ is.

solve.answer: She made a counting mistake, because a probability cannot be greater than 1.
solve.work: 12/10 > 1, impossible as a probability; favourable outcomes cannot exceed total.

questions.skill: Compare and order probabilities
questions.stem: Which of these probabilities belongs to the most likely event?
questions.solution: As decimals the numbers are 0.625, 0.6, about 0.583 and 0.62. The greatest is 0.625, which is $\frac{5}{8}$.

questions.skill: Compare and order probabilities
questions.stem: How many of these probabilities are greater than $\frac{1}{2}$? $0.55$, $\frac{3}{8}$, $\frac{7}{10}$, $0.5$, $\frac{4}{9}$, $0.99$
questions.solution: Compare each with 0.5. 0.55, 0.7 and 0.99 are greater. $\frac{3}{8}$ = 0.375 and $\frac{4}{9}$ is about 0.44 are less, and 0.5 is equal. So 3 are greater.

questions.skill: Interpret a probability in a situation
questions.stem: A bag holds 20 marbles, each red or blue. The probability of picking a red marble at random is 0, and the probability of picking a blue marble is 1. Which must be true?
choices: Every one of the 20 marbles is red.
Every one of the 20 marbles is blue.
Most of the 20 marbles are blue, but not all.
Half of the 20 marbles are red and half are blue.
questions.answer: Every one of the 20 marbles is blue.
questions.solution: A probability of 0 for red means no marble can be red. A probability of 1 for blue means every marble is blue.

solve.answer: Every one of the 20 marbles is blue.
solve.work: P(red)=0 means no red; all 20 blue.

questions.skill: Find a probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.stem: A bag holds 6 red marbles, 3 blue marbles and 1 green marble. One marble is picked at random. Which statement is true?
choices: Blue is more likely than red and green together.
Green and blue are equally likely.
Red is more likely than blue and green together.
The probability of red is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.
questions.answer: Red is more likely than blue and green together.
questions.solution: There are 10 marbles. Red has probability $\frac{6}{10}$, and blue and green together have $\frac{4}{10}$. So red is more likely than the other two together, and its probability is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$.

solve.answer: Red is more likely than blue and green together.
solve.work: Red 6/10 vs blue+green 4/10: red more likely. P(red)=0.6 not < 1/2; blue 3/10 < red+green 7/10; green 1/10 != blue 3/10.

questions.skill: Find a probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.stem: A bag holds 24 marbles. The probability of picking a green marble at random is $\frac{1}{6}$. How many of the marbles are green?
questions.solution: Green marbles are $\frac{1}{6}$ of the 24 marbles. 24 / 6 = 4 marbles.

questions.skill: Find a probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.stem: A raffle has 40 tickets. The probability that a ticket drawn at random wins a prize is 0.15. How many of the tickets win a prize?
questions.solution: The winning tickets are 0.15 of the 40 tickets. 0.15 times 40 = 6 tickets.

questions.skill: Compare and order probabilities
questions.stem: A fair coin and a fair six-sided die are used. Event A: the coin lands on heads. Event B: the die shows a number less than 7. Event C: the die shows a 6. Event D: the die shows a number greater than 6. Which list puts the events in order from least likely to most likely?
questions.solution: D is impossible (probability 0). C has probability $\frac{1}{6}$. A has probability $\frac{1}{2}$. B is certain (probability 1). So the order is D, C, A, B.

questions.skill: Describe an event from its probability
questions.stem: Event Y is more likely to happen than not. Event X is more likely to happen than Event Y. Which pair could be the probabilities of X and Y, in that order?
questions.solution: More likely than not means a probability greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, so Y is above $0.5$. X is more likely than Y, so X has the greater probability, and it cannot be more than 1. Only $0.9$ for X and $0.7$ for Y fits. The pair $0.7$ and $0.9$ is in the wrong order, $0.4$ and $0.3$ are both below $\frac{1}{2}$, and $1.3$ is not a probability.

solve.work: Y more likely than not: P(Y) > 0.5. X more likely than Y: P(X) > P(Y). 0.9 and 0.7: 0.7 > 0.5 and 0.9 > 0.7, valid. 0.4/0.3: Y < 0.5. 0.7/0.9: X < Y. 1.3 is not a probability.

questions.skill: experimental probability from a count
questions.stem: Mia spun a spinner 20 times. It landed on red 7 times. What is the experimental probability that the spinner lands on red? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Experimental probability = (times the event happened) / (number of trials) = 7/20.

questions.skill: probabilities of an outcome and its complement
questions.stem: A coin was tossed 50 times and landed heads 22 times. What is the experimental probability that the coin lands tails?
questions.solution: The coin landed tails 50 - 22 = 28 times. The experimental probability of tails is 28/50.

questions.skill: experimental probability from a count
questions.stem: A basketball player made 18 of her 24 free throws in practice. Based on this, what is the experimental probability that she makes a free throw? Write your answer as a decimal.

questions.skill: experimental and theoretical probability
questions.stem: Which is the correct way to find the experimental probability of an event?
choices: Divide the number of times the event happened by the total number of trials.
Divide the total number of trials by the number of times the event happened.
Divide the number of favorable outcomes by the number of equally likely outcomes.
Divide the number of times the event happened by the number of times it did not happen.
questions.answer: Divide the number of times the event happened by the total number of trials.
questions.solution: Experimental probability compares what actually happened in an experiment: the number of times the event occurred divided by the total number of trials. The other methods give the inverse, the theoretical probability, or the odds.

solve.answer: Divide the number of times the event happened by the total number of trials.
solve.work: Experimental probability = times event happened / total trials.

questions.skill: predicting a count from experimental probability
questions.stem: In a long experiment, a spinner landed on blue $\frac{1}{4}$ of the time. If the spinner is spun 80 more times, about how many times would you predict it to land on blue?
questions.solution: Predicted number = 1/4 of 80 = 20.

questions.skill: experimental probability from a table or list of outcomes
questions.stem: A paper cup was tossed 25 times. It landed on its side 15 times, upside down 6 times and upright 4 times. What is the experimental probability that the cup lands upright? Write your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The cup landed upright 4 times out of 25: 4/25 = 0.16.

questions.skill: experimental probability as a fraction, decimal or percent
questions.stem: It rained on 12 of the last 30 days. Based on this, which is the experimental probability that it rains on a day?
questions.solution: 12 rainy days out of 30 days gives 12/30 = 2/5. The fraction 2/3 compares rainy days with dry days (12 to 18), and 3/5 is the probability of a dry day.

questions.skill: predicting a count from experimental probability
questions.stem: In a survey of 50 randomly chosen shoppers, 10 bought a drink. Based on this survey, predict how many of 400 shoppers would buy a drink.
questions.solution: The experimental probability is 10/50 = 1/5. Then 1/5 of 400 = 80.

questions.skill: experimental probability as a fraction, decimal or percent
questions.stem: A player made 9 of her 20 shots. What is her experimental probability of making a shot, written as a percent?
questions.solution: 9/20 = 45/100 = 45%. The 55% is the percent of shots she missed.

questions.skill: experimental probability from a count
questions.stem: A coin was flipped 8 times. The results, in order, were H, T, T, H, T, H, T, T. What is the experimental probability of getting heads? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Heads came up 3 times in 8 flips, so the experimental probability is 3/8.

questions.skill: experimental probability from a count
questions.stem: A factory tested 250 light bulbs and found that 5 were defective. What is the experimental probability that a bulb chosen at random is defective? Write your answer as a decimal.

questions.skill: predicting a count from experimental probability
questions.stem: In a test, 51 of 60 seeds sprouted. Based on this test, about how many of 500 seeds would you predict will sprout?
questions.solution: The experimental probability is 51/60 = 0.85. Then 0.85 x 500 = 425.

questions.skill: working backward to find trials or successes
questions.stem: A spinner landed on yellow 18 times. This was an experimental probability of 0.3 for yellow. How many times was the spinner spun?
questions.solution: Number of spins x 0.3 = 18, so the number of spins is 18 / 0.3 = 60.

questions.skill: experimental and theoretical probability
questions.stem: A fair coin was tossed 10 times and landed heads 7 times. Which statement is correct?
choices: The experimental probability of heads is $\frac{1}{2}$ and the theoretical probability is $\frac{7}{10}$.
The experimental probability of heads is $\frac{3}{10}$ and the theoretical probability is $\frac{1}{2}$.
The experimental probability of heads is $\frac{7}{10}$ and the theoretical probability is $\frac{3}{10}$.
The experimental probability of heads is $\frac{7}{10}$ and the theoretical probability is $\frac{1}{2}$.
questions.answer: The experimental probability of heads is $\frac{7}{10}$ and the theoretical probability is $\frac{1}{2}$.
questions.solution: The experimental probability comes from what happened: 7 heads in 10 tosses, 7/10. The theoretical probability for a fair coin is 1/2.

solve.answer: The experimental probability of heads is $\frac{7}{10}$ and the theoretical probability is $\frac{1}{2}$.
solve.work: Experimental 7/10; a fair coin has theoretical 1/2.

questions.skill: experimental probability from a table or list of outcomes
questions.stem: A spinner with three colors was spun 40 times. It landed on red 14 times, on blue 18 times and on green 8 times. What is the experimental probability that it lands on red or green? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Red or green happened 14 + 8 = 22 times in 40 spins: 22/40 = 11/20.

questions.skill: predicting a count from experimental probability
questions.stem: In a survey, 20 of 80 students said they walk to school. At a school with 600 students, about how many students would you predict walk to school?
questions.solution: The experimental probability is 20/80 = 1/4. Then 1/4 of 600 = 150.

questions.skill: predicting a count from experimental probability
questions.stem: A baseball player got 36 hits in 120 times at bat. At this rate, how many hits would you expect in 250 times at bat?

questions.skill: experimental probability as a fraction, decimal or percent
questions.stem: Priya tossed a thumbtack 100 times. It landed point up 38 times and point down the other times. What is the experimental probability that it lands point down?
questions.solution: It landed point down 100 - 38 = 62 times, so the probability is 62/100 = 0.62.

questions.skill: predicting a count from experimental probability
questions.stem: The experimental probability that a bolt from a machine is defective is 0.04. About how many defective bolts would you expect in a shipment of 2,500 bolts?

questions.skill: experimental probability from a table or list of outcomes
questions.stem: A number cube was rolled 30 times. The 1 came up 4 times, the 2 came up 6 times, the 3 came up 5 times, the 4 came up 7 times, the 5 came up 3 times and the 6 came up 5 times. What is the experimental probability of rolling an even number?
questions.solution: Even numbers came up 6 + 7 + 5 = 18 times in 30 rolls: 18/30 = 3/5. The value 1/2 is the theoretical probability, and 2/5 is the probability of an odd number.

questions.skill: predicting in a multi-step problem
questions.stem: A spinner has sections A, B and C. In 60 spins it landed on A 24 times and on B 15 times; all the other spins landed on C. Based on these results, how many times would you predict the spinner to land on C in 200 spins?
questions.solution: C came up 60 - 24 - 15 = 21 times in 60 spins, so its experimental probability is 21/60 = 7/20. Then 7/20 of 200 = 70.

questions.skill: experimental and theoretical probability
questions.stem: Anna tossed a paper cup 10 times and Ben tossed the same kind of cup 200 times. Each recorded how often it landed upright. Whose experimental probability is more likely to be close to the cup's true probability, and why?
choices: Anna, because results from fewer trials tend to be closer to the true probability.
Ben, because results from more trials tend to be closer to the true probability.
Ben, because results from more trials are always exactly equal to the true probability.
Neither, because the number of trials does not affect how close the result is.
questions.answer: Ben, because results from more trials tend to be closer to the true probability.
questions.solution: With more trials, an experimental probability tends to settle near the true probability, though it need not equal it exactly. So Ben's 200 tosses are more likely to be close.

solve.answer: Ben, because results from more trials tend to be closer to the true probability.
solve.work: Larger samples tend to be closer to the true probability (not always exactly equal).

questions.skill: working backward to find trials or successes
questions.stem: A basketball player makes 3 out of every 8 free throws in practice. Based on this, about how many free throws would she need to take to expect to make 18?
questions.solution: She makes 3/8 of her shots, so shots x 3/8 = 18, and shots = 18 / (3/8) = 18 x 8/3 = 48.

questions.skill: combining the data of several experiments
questions.stem: A coin was flipped 40 times and landed heads 18 times. It was then flipped 60 more times and landed heads 33 times. What is the experimental probability of heads for all 100 flips together?
questions.solution: Heads came up 18 + 33 = 51 times in 40 + 60 = 100 flips: 51/100 = 0.51. Averaging 0.45 and 0.55 gives 0.50, which ignores that the two sets have different sizes.

questions.skill: predicting in a multi-step problem
questions.stem: On a bus route, the experimental probability that a bus is late is 0.12. If a bus makes 250 trips, how many of them would you expect to be on time?
questions.solution: The probability of being on time is 1 - 0.12 = 0.88, and 0.88 x 250 = 220.

questions.skill: estimating an unknown quantity from a sample
questions.stem: A bag holds 20 marbles, some red and the rest blue. Maya drew a marble 50 times, putting it back each time, and drew red 35 times. Based on this, what is the best estimate of the number of red marbles in the bag?
questions.solution: The experimental probability of red is 35/50 = 0.7, so about 0.7 x 20 = 14 of the marbles are red. The number 6 is the estimate for blue.

questions.skill: combining the data of several experiments
questions.stem: A quality inspector found 6 defective parts in a batch of 80 parts, and 9 defective parts in a batch of 120 parts. Using the data from both batches together, how many defective parts would you expect in a shipment of 1,000 parts?
questions.solution: Together there were 15 defective parts in 200 parts, so the experimental probability is 15/200 = 0.075. Then 0.075 x 1,000 = 75.

questions.skill: probabilities of an outcome and its complement
questions.stem: A spinner has four colors, and these are all the possible outcomes. In an experiment, the experimental probabilities were 0.30 for red, 0.25 for blue and 0.20 for green. What is the experimental probability for yellow?
questions.solution: The probabilities of all outcomes add to 1. Yellow is 1 - 0.30 - 0.25 - 0.20 = 0.25.

questions.skill: comparing and matching experimental probabilities
questions.stem: Team A won 14 of its first 20 games. Team B won 21 of its first 35 games. If each team plays 100 more games and wins at the same rate as before, how many more games is Team A predicted to win than Team B?
questions.solution: Team A wins 14/20 = 0.7 of its games: 70 of 100. Team B wins 21/35 = 0.6 of its games: 60 of 100. The difference is 70 - 60 = 10.

questions.skill: comparing and matching experimental probabilities
questions.stem: Which set of results gives an experimental probability of $\frac{2}{5}$?
choices: The event happened 15 times in 25 trials.
The event happened 14 times in 21 trials.
The event happened 14 times in 35 trials.
The event happened 25 times in 40 trials.
questions.answer: The event happened 14 times in 35 trials.

solve.answer: The event happened 14 times in 35 trials.

questions.skill: Find a probability in a uniform model
questions.stem: A fair spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. What is the probability that it lands on 4?
questions.solution: The 5 outcomes are equally likely, so each has probability $\frac{1}{5}$.

questions.skill: Recognize a uniform or valid probability model
questions.stem: Which is the probability model for one roll of a fair six-sided number cube?
choices: Each of the numbers 1 to 6 has probability $\frac{1}{5}$
Each of the numbers 1 to 6 has probability $\frac{1}{3}$
Each of the numbers 1 to 6 has probability $\frac{1}{6}$
Each of the numbers 1 to 6 has probability $\frac{1}{2}$
questions.answer: Each of the numbers 1 to 6 has probability $\frac{1}{6}$
questions.solution: A fair cube has 6 equally likely outcomes, so each has probability $\frac{1}{6}$. The six probabilities add up to 1.

solve.answer: Each of the numbers 1 to 6 has probability $\frac{1}{6}$

questions.skill: Find a missing probability in a model
questions.stem: A spinner can land on red, blue or green. The probability of red is 0.3 and the probability of blue is 0.5. What is the probability of green?
questions.solution: The probabilities in a model add up to 1. So green is $1 - 0.3 - 0.5 = 0.2$.

questions.skill: Find a probability in a uniform model
questions.stem: A fair number cube is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
questions.solution: The numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, which is 2 of the 6 equally likely outcomes: $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.skill: Predict how often an outcome will occur
questions.stem: A fair coin is flipped 50 times. How many heads should you predict?
questions.solution: The probability of heads is $\frac{1}{2}$. So predict $\frac{1}{2} \times 50 = 25$ heads.

questions.skill: Find a relative frequency
questions.stem: Sam flips a coin 20 times and gets 12 heads. What is the relative frequency of heads?
questions.solution: The relative frequency is the number of heads divided by the number of flips: $\frac{12}{20} = \frac{3}{5}$.

questions.skill: Recognize a uniform or valid probability model
questions.stem: Which situation is best modeled by a uniform probability model?
choices: Whether a thumbtack tossed in the air lands point up
Whether a basketball player makes her next free throw
The color of the next car to drive past a school
Picking 1 of 8 identical name slips from a hat at random
questions.answer: Picking 1 of 8 identical name slips from a hat at random
questions.solution: A uniform model needs equally likely outcomes. Each of the 8 identical slips is equally likely to be picked. The other situations have outcomes that are not equally likely.

solve.answer: Picking 1 of 8 identical name slips from a hat at random
solve.work: Identical slips drawn at random: each equally likely (1/8). Others are not equally likely outcomes.

questions.skill: Recognize a uniform or valid probability model
questions.stem: Which list of numbers could be the probabilities of outcomes A, B, C and D in a probability model?
questions.solution: The probabilities must each be between 0 and 1 and add up to 1. Only 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 1 with no negative number. The others add to more than 1, or include a negative probability.

solve.work: Sums: 1.1, 1.4, has a negative, 1.0. Only 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 is valid.

questions.skill: Find a probability in a uniform model
questions.stem: A bag holds 3 red, 5 blue and 2 yellow marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
questions.solution: There are 10 marbles and 5 are blue, so the probability is $\frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}$.

questions.skill: Predict how often an outcome will occur
questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sections, and 2 of them are shaded. If it is spun 40 times, how many times should you predict it lands on a shaded section?
questions.solution: The probability of shaded is $\frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$. So predict $\frac{1}{4} \times 40 = 10$ times.

questions.skill: Find a missing probability in a model
questions.stem: A spinner has four colors. The probabilities are red 0.35, blue 0.25 and green 0.15. What is the probability of yellow?
questions.solution: The four probabilities add up to 1. The first three add to 0.75, so yellow is $1 - 0.75 = 0.25$.

questions.skill: Compare an observed frequency with the model probability
questions.stem: A fair number cube is rolled 60 times, and a 4 lands 14 times. How does the relative frequency of a 4 compare with the model probability of a 4?
choices: The relative frequency is $\frac{14}{60}$, which is lower than the model probability of $\frac{1}{6}$
The relative frequency is $\frac{14}{6}$, which is higher than the model probability of $\frac{1}{6}$
The relative frequency is $\frac{14}{60}$, which is equal to the model probability of $\frac{1}{6}$
The relative frequency is $\frac{14}{60}$, which is higher than the model probability of $\frac{1}{6}$
questions.answer: The relative frequency is $\frac{14}{60}$, which is higher than the model probability of $\frac{1}{6}$
questions.solution: The relative frequency is $\frac{14}{60} \approx 0.233$. The model probability is $\frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167$. So the relative frequency is higher.

solve.answer: The relative frequency is $\frac{14}{60}$, which is higher than the model probability of $\frac{1}{6}$

questions.skill: Predict how often an outcome will occur
questions.stem: A weighted coin lands heads with probability 0.6. How many heads should you predict in 150 flips?
questions.solution: Predict the probability times the number of flips: $0.6 \times 150 = 90$ heads.

questions.skill: Find a relative frequency
questions.stem: A spinner is spun 30 times. It lands on red 12 times, on blue 10 times and on green 8 times. What is the relative frequency of blue?
questions.solution: The relative frequency of blue is $\frac{10}{30} = \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.skill: Build a non-uniform probability model
questions.stem: A bag holds 2 red, 3 blue and 5 green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. Which gives the probability model?
questions.solution: There are 10 marbles. The probabilities are $\frac{2}{10}$, $\frac{3}{10}$ and $\frac{5}{10}$, which are 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5. The colors are not equally likely.

questions.skill: Find a probability in a uniform model
questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sections numbered 1 to 8. What is the probability that it lands on an odd number or on a number greater than 6?
questions.solution: The favorable numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7 (odd) and 8 (greater than 6, not already counted). That is 5 of 8 outcomes: $\frac{5}{8}$.

questions.skill: Find the probability of an event in a non-uniform model
questions.stem: A loaded number cube has these probabilities: 1 is 0.1, 2 is 0.1, 3 is 0.2, 4 is 0.2, 5 is 0.15 and 6 is 0.25. What is the probability of rolling an even number?
questions.solution: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6. Add their probabilities: $0.1 + 0.2 + 0.25 = 0.55$.

questions.skill: Judge whether a model fits observed data
questions.stem: Ben flips a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. He says, "The model says heads has probability 50%, so this coin must be unfair." Which response is best?
choices: Not necessarily; 10 flips is too few to judge, so he should flip more times
Yes; a fair coin must land on heads exactly half of the time
Yes; 7 heads is more than 5, so the model must be wrong
No; the model is right, so the result cannot be a coincidence
questions.answer: Not necessarily; 10 flips is too few to judge, so he should flip more times
questions.solution: With few trials the relative frequency can differ a lot from the probability just by chance. More flips would give better evidence.

solve.answer: Not necessarily; 10 flips is too few to judge, so he should flip more times
solve.work: 7 of 10 is quite possible with a fair coin; small samples vary, so more flips are needed.

questions.skill: Predict how often an outcome will occur
questions.stem: A fair number cube is rolled 90 times. How many times should you predict a 5 or a 6?
questions.solution: The probability of a 5 or a 6 is $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$. So predict $\frac{1}{3} \times 90 = 30$ times.

questions.skill: Compare observed counts with the predicted counts
questions.stem: A spinner has 4 equal sections. It is spun 40 times. The sections land 8, 12, 9 and 11 times. By how many does the count of 12 differ from the predicted count for that section?
questions.solution: Each section is predicted to land $\frac{1}{4} \times 40 = 10$ times. The count of 12 is $12 - 10 = 2$ more than predicted.

questions.skill: Estimate a probability from observed frequencies
questions.stem: A thumbtack is tossed 200 times and lands point up 126 times. Use the relative frequency to estimate the probability that it lands point up. Write your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The estimated probability is the relative frequency: $\frac{126}{200} = 0.63$.

questions.skill: Predict how often an outcome will occur
questions.stem: A thumbtack landed point up in 126 of 200 tosses. Using that relative frequency as the probability, how many times should you predict it lands point up in 500 tosses?
questions.solution: The probability is $\frac{126}{200} = 0.63$. So predict $0.63 \times 500 = 315$ times.

questions.skill: Build a non-uniform probability model
questions.stem: A spinner lands on red, blue or green. The probability of red is 3 times the probability of blue, and green has the same probability as blue. What is the probability of red? Write a fraction.
questions.solution: Let blue be $p$. Then green is $p$ and red is $3p$, so $p + p + 3p = 1$ and $p = \frac{1}{5}$. Red is $3p = \frac{3}{5}$.

solve.work: Let blue = b, green = b, red = 3b; 5b = 1, b = 1/5, red = 3/5.

questions.skill: Compare observed counts with the predicted counts
questions.stem: A spinner has 4 equal sections. In 80 spins, red lands 30 times. How does 30 compare with the count that the model predicts for red?
questions.solution: The model predicts $\frac{1}{4} \times 80 = 20$ red. The observed 30 is $30 - 20 = 10$ more.

questions.skill: Judge whether a model fits observed data
questions.stem: A number cube is rolled 60 times. These are the counts for the faces 1 to 6. Which set of counts gives the strongest reason to doubt that the cube is fair?
questions.solution: A fair cube predicts about 10 of each face. The counts 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 25 are far from 10 and keep growing, which is unlikely by chance. The others stay close to 10.

solve.work: Fair predicts 10 each. 2,3,5,10,15,25 (sum 60) is far from uniform; the others are close or exact.

questions.skill: Estimate a probability from observed frequencies
questions.stem: In 50 draws with replacement from a bag of 20 marbles, a red marble was drawn 15 times. Use the relative frequency to estimate how many of the 20 marbles are red.
questions.solution: The estimated probability of red is $\frac{15}{50} = 0.3$. So about $0.3 \times 20 = 6$ marbles are red.

questions.skill: Build a non-uniform probability model
questions.stem: A weighted number cube lands on 6 with probability 0.3. The other five numbers are equally likely. What is the probability of rolling a 2? Write a decimal.
questions.solution: The other five numbers share $1 - 0.3 = 0.7$ equally, so each has probability $0.7 \div 5 = 0.14$.

questions.skill: Judge whether a model fits observed data
questions.stem: Which statement about relative frequency and probability is true?
choices: After 100 trials, the relative frequency always equals the probability
More trials make the relative frequency tend toward the probability
After three heads in a row, tails becomes more likely on the next flip
Because results vary, a probability model cannot be used to make predictions
questions.answer: More trials make the relative frequency tend toward the probability
questions.solution: With more trials the relative frequency tends to settle near the probability, though it need not match it exactly. Past results do not change the next flip, and models still give useful predictions.

solve.answer: More trials make the relative frequency tend toward the probability
solve.work: Law of large numbers: more trials tend toward probability. Others are false.

questions.skill: Compare an observed frequency with the model probability
questions.stem: A spinner has 5 equal sections. It is spun 120 times and section 3 lands 36 times. By how much does the relative frequency of section 3 exceed the model probability of section 3? Write a decimal.
questions.solution: The relative frequency is $\frac{36}{120} = 0.3$. The model probability is $\frac{1}{5} = 0.2$. The difference is $0.3 - 0.2 = 0.1$.

questions.skill: Compare observed counts with the predicted counts
questions.stem: In 40 flips a coin lands heads 28 times, so a student models the probability of heads as 0.7. In 100 new flips it lands heads 62 times. Which comparison is correct?
choices: The model predicts 70 heads, and 62 is 8 more than predicted
The model predicts 30 heads, and 62 is 32 more than predicted
The model predicts 28 heads, and 62 is 34 more than predicted
The model predicts 70 heads, and 62 is 8 fewer than predicted
questions.answer: The model predicts 70 heads, and 62 is 8 fewer than predicted
questions.solution: The model predicts $0.7 \times 100 = 70$ heads. The observed 62 is $70 - 62 = 8$ fewer than predicted.

solve.answer: The model predicts 70 heads, and 62 is 8 fewer than predicted

questions.skill: Count the outcomes of a compound event
questions.stem: A coin is flipped two times. How many different outcomes are possible?
questions.solution: List them: heads-heads, heads-tails, tails-heads, tails-tails. That is 4 outcomes.

questions.skill: Count the outcomes of a compound event
questions.stem: A coin is flipped and a number cube (numbered 1 to 6) is rolled. How many different outcomes are possible?
questions.solution: Each of the 2 coin results can go with each of the 6 numbers: 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes.

questions.skill: Probability from a list of coin outcomes
questions.stem: A coin is flipped two times. What is the probability that it lands heads both times?
questions.solution: The 4 equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Only HH is heads both times, so the probability is $\frac{1}{4}$.

questions.skill: List the sample space
questions.stem: Which list shows all the possible outcomes when a coin is flipped two times? (H means heads and T means tails.)
questions.solution: The first flip can be H or T, and so can the second. That gives HH, HT, TH and TT. The other lists leave outcomes out.

solve.work: The full sample space: HH, HT, TH, TT.

questions.skill: Count the outcomes of a compound event
questions.stem: A spinner has 3 equal sections: red, blue and green. It is spun two times. How many different outcomes are possible? (Red then blue is different from blue then red.)
questions.solution: There are 3 results for the first spin and 3 for the second: 3 × 3 = 9 outcomes.

questions.skill: Probability from a list of coin outcomes
questions.stem: Nina tosses two coins. What is the probability that at least one of the coins lands heads?
questions.solution: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Three of the four have at least one head (HH, HT, TH), so the probability is $\frac{3}{4}$. HT and TH are two different outcomes, so do not count them as one.

questions.skill: Probability of a coin and a number cube
questions.stem: A fair coin is flipped and a fair number cube numbered 1 to 6 is rolled. What is the probability of getting heads and a 6?
questions.solution: There are 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes, and only one of them is heads with a 6. The probability is $\frac{1}{12}$.

questions.skill: Count the outcomes of a compound event
questions.stem: A tree diagram shows lunch choices. The first branches are the sandwich: ham, turkey or cheese. From each sandwich, the second branches are the drink: water or juice. How many complete lunches (paths from start to end) does the tree show?
questions.solution: Each of the 3 sandwiches branches into 2 drinks, so there are 3 × 2 = 6 paths.

questions.skill: Count the outcomes of a compound event
questions.stem: A coin is flipped 3 times. How many different outcomes are possible?
questions.solution: Each flip has 2 results, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes.

questions.skill: Estimate a probability with a simulation
questions.stem: Mia uses a number cube to act out a coin flip. An odd number means heads and an even number means tails. She rolls a 4. What does her roll stand for?
questions.solution: 4 is an even number, and even numbers stand for tails.

solve.work: 4 is even, so it stands for tails.

questions.skill: Probability from a table of two number cubes
questions.stem: Two fair number cubes, each numbered 1 to 6, are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
questions.solution: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. The sums of 7 are 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2 and 6+1, which is 6 outcomes. The probability is $\frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$.

questions.skill: Probability from a table of two number cubes
questions.stem: Dara rolls two fair number cubes, each numbered 1 to 6, and adds the numbers. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
questions.solution: Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, the sums of 8 are 2+6, 3+5, 4+4, 5+3 and 6+2. That is 5 outcomes, so the probability is $\frac{5}{36}$.

questions.skill: Probability of stages in a tree diagram
questions.stem: A bag has 3 red marbles and 2 blue marbles. A marble is drawn and put back, and then a second marble is drawn. What is the probability that both marbles are red?
questions.solution: Each draw is red with probability $\frac{3}{5}$, because the first marble is put back. Both red: $\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{9}{25}$.

questions.skill: Probability from a table of two spinners
questions.stem: A fair spinner has 4 equal sections numbered 1 to 4. It is spun two times and the numbers are added. What is the probability that the sum is 5?
questions.solution: There are 4 × 4 = 16 equally likely outcomes. The sums of 5 are 1+4, 2+3, 3+2 and 4+1, which is 4 outcomes. The probability is $\frac{4}{16} = \frac{1}{4}$.

questions.skill: Estimate a probability with a simulation
questions.stem: A basketball player makes about half of her free throws. To act out two shots, a coin is flipped two times, and heads means a made shot. In 20 trials of two flips, both flips were heads in 6 of the trials. Based on the trials, what is the estimated probability that she makes both shots?
questions.solution: The estimate is the number of trials with both heads divided by all the trials: $\frac{6}{20} = \frac{3}{10}$.

questions.skill: Estimate a probability with a simulation
questions.stem: A bag holds 4 marbles of different colors, and one is drawn at random. Which model could act out this draw?
choices: Spin a spinner with 4 equal sections
Spin a spinner with 3 equal sections
questions.answer: Spin a spinner with 4 equal sections
questions.solution: The model needs 4 equally likely results, one for each marble. A spinner with 4 equal sections gives that. A coin has 2 results, a number cube has 6, and the other spinner has 3.

solve.answer: Spin a spinner with 4 equal sections
solve.work: 4 equally likely outcomes: a spinner with 4 equal sections.

questions.skill: Probability from a list of coin outcomes
questions.stem: A family plans to have 3 children. Each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl. What is the probability that all three children are girls?
questions.solution: There are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 equally likely outcomes, and only one (girl, girl, girl) has all girls. The probability is $\frac{1}{8}$.

questions.skill: Probability from a list of coin outcomes
questions.stem: A fair coin is flipped three times. What is the probability that at least one flip is tails?
questions.solution: Of the 8 equally likely outcomes, only HHH has no tails. So 7 of the 8 outcomes have at least one tail, and the probability is $\frac{7}{8}$.

questions.skill: Probability from a table of two spinners
questions.stem: Spinner A has three equal sections numbered 1, 2 and 3. Spinner B also has three equal sections numbered 1, 2 and 3. Each is spun once and the two numbers are added. What is the probability that the sum is even?
questions.solution: There are 9 equally likely pairs. An even sum comes from 1+1, 1+3, 2+2, 3+1 and 3+3, which is 5 pairs. The probability is $\frac{5}{9}$.

questions.skill: Probability of a coin and a number cube
questions.stem: A fair number cube numbered 1 to 6 is rolled and a fair coin is flipped. What is the probability of rolling an even number and getting heads?
questions.solution: The chance of an even number is $\frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ and the chance of heads is $\frac{1}{2}$. Both: $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$. (Equivalently, 3 of the 12 outcomes.)

questions.skill: Probability of stages in a tree diagram
questions.stem: A bag has 2 red marbles and 2 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn one after the other, without putting the first one back. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.solution: The first marble is red with probability $\frac{2}{4}$. Then 1 red is left among 3 marbles, so the second is red with probability $\frac{1}{3}$. Both: $\frac{2}{4} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6}$.

questions.skill: Probability of stages in a tree diagram
questions.stem: A bag has 3 green marbles and 2 yellow marbles. Two marbles are drawn one after the other, without putting the first one back. What is the probability that the two marbles are different colors?
questions.solution: Green then yellow: $\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{2}{4} = \frac{3}{10}$. Yellow then green: $\frac{2}{5} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{3}{10}$. Add the two paths: $\frac{3}{10} + \frac{3}{10} = \frac{3}{5}$.

questions.skill: Probability from a table of two number cubes
questions.stem: Two fair number cubes, each numbered 1 to 6, are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is less than 5?
questions.solution: Sums less than 5 are 2, 3 and 4. Sum 2 has 1 outcome, sum 3 has 2 outcomes and sum 4 has 3 outcomes: 6 in all out of 36. The probability is $\frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$.

questions.skill: Count the outcomes of a compound event
questions.stem: A code has one letter chosen from A, B, C or D, followed by two digits. Each digit is chosen from 1, 2 or 3, and a digit may be used twice. How many different codes are possible?
questions.solution: There are 4 choices for the letter, 3 for the first digit and 3 for the second digit: 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 codes.

questions.skill: Probability of stages in a tree diagram
questions.stem: The chance of rain on Saturday is $\frac{1}{4}$ and the chance of rain on Sunday is $\frac{1}{3}$. The two days do not affect each other. What is the probability that it does not rain on either day?
questions.solution: No rain on Saturday: $1 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$. No rain on Sunday: $1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}$. Both: $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$.

solve.work: No rain Sat 3/4, no rain Sun 2/3: 3/4 x 2/3 = 1/2.

questions.skill: Estimate a probability with a simulation
questions.stem: A forecast says there is a 20% chance of rain on each of 2 days. To act this out, a random digit from 0 to 9 is used for each day: 0 or 1 means rain, and 2 to 9 means no rain. Ten trials, each a pair of digits (day 1, day 2), are: 03, 41, 17, 82, 55, 10, 96, 71, 28, 64. Based on these trials, what is the estimated probability that it rains on both days?
questions.solution: Rain on both days needs both digits to be 0 or 1. Only the pair 10 qualifies, out of 10 trials. The estimate is $\frac{1}{10}$.

solve.work: Both digits 0 or 1: 03 no, 41 no, 17 no, 82 no, 55 no, 10 yes, 96 no, 71 no, 28 no, 64 no. 1 of 10 = 1/10.

questions.skill: Estimate a probability with a simulation
questions.stem: A coin flipped three times is acted out with random digits: an even digit means heads and an odd digit means tails. Eight trials, each of three digits, are: 246, 135, 482, 713, 668, 902, 357, 841. Based on these trials, what is the estimated probability of getting three heads?
questions.solution: Three heads needs all three digits even. That happens in 246, 482 and 668, which is 3 of the 8 trials. The estimate is $\frac{3}{8}$. (902 and 841 each have an odd digit.)

solve.work: All three digits even: 246 yes, 135 no, 482 yes, 713 no, 668 yes, 902 no (9 odd), 357 no, 841 no. 3/8.

questions.skill: List the sample space
questions.stem: A coin is flipped three times. Which list shows all the outcomes with exactly two heads? (H means heads and T means tails.)
questions.solution: Exactly two heads and one tail: the tail can be in the third, second or first place, giving HHT, HTH and THH. HHH has three heads, and HTT, THT and TTH have only one.

solve.work: Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH.

questions.skill: Probability from a table of two number cubes
questions.stem: Two fair number cubes, each numbered 1 to 6, are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is 12?
questions.solution: The products of 12 are 2×6, 6×2, 3×4 and 4×3, which is 4 outcomes out of 36. The probability is $\frac{4}{36} = \frac{1}{9}$.

questions.skill: Probability from a table of two spinners
questions.stem: Spinner A has four equal sections numbered 1 to 4. Spinner B has three equal sections numbered 1 to 3. Each is spun once. What is the probability that the number on spinner A is greater than the number on spinner B?
questions.solution: There are 4 × 3 = 12 equally likely pairs. A = 2 beats B = 1 (1 pair). A = 3 beats B = 1 or 2 (2 pairs). A = 4 beats B = 1, 2 or 3 (3 pairs). That is 6 of 12, so the probability is $\frac{1}{2}$.
